abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers powerful approaches for identifying multivariate patterns in neuroimaging data, yet the biological validity and interpretability of the discriminative patterns learned by such models remain incompletely understood. Here, we benchmarked multiple ML approaches for sex classification across development (8-21 years) on structural neuroimaging data and investigated the effects of age on model performance and feature stability. Linear and nonlinear models demonstrated comparable classification performance, indicating that high predictive accuracy can be achieved without relying on highly complex architectures; however, age-stratified analyses and cross-age generalization tests demonstrated that developmental stage influences classification performance, and consistency of learned neuroanatomical features. To assess biological interpretability, we applied SHAP and LIME explainability methods and developed a comprehensive framework for translating feature attributions into biologically interpretable patterns. Sex-discriminative regions were distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical structures and exhibited marked developmental variation. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of interpretable ML for developmental neuroimaging and highlight the importance of evaluating predictive performance while simultaneously taking biological validity, developmental specificity, and attribution stability into consideration.
